method_source: GraphRAG-style Local Evidence Aggregation: deterministic graph-window retrieval with the SA-MCGS local evidence schema, without relation-first memory, critical-pair revisiting, OC/core signals, or dynamic-core replacement.
deterministic_window_policy: one center node plus deterministic graph neighbors; fill by SCC order

conflicts.description: §275 provides grounds for excluding performance, while §283 allows for damage claims based on that exclusion. If performance is excluded, but damage claims are still valid, this could create a conflict in enforcement unless clearly defined.

Both address damages instead of performance, but bgb_280 requires a prior deadline, while bgb_282 allows damages if the performance is no longer tolerable. This could lead to conflicting interpretations in practice.
bgb_280 outlines general conditions for damages, while bgb_281 adds specific requirements like a prior deadline. This could lead to ambiguity in determining when damages are applicable.
Bgb_281 introduces a cure requirement with a 20% charge, while bgb_283 allows Schadensersatz statt der Leistung without cure, creating a conflict in how the same obligation is handled.
Bgb_281 requires a cure with a 20% charge, while bgb_311a allows immediate Schadensersatz without cure, creating a conflict in the same path.

§280 restricts damages in lieu of performance to specific conditions, while §281 outlines the conditions under which such damages can be claimed. This creates potential for conflict if the conditions of §280 are not clearly met.

§280 restricts damages in lieu of performance to specific conditions, while §282 allows such damages when the debtor violates §241(2). This could create a conflict if the conditions of §280 are not fully satisfied.

§280 restricts damages in lieu of performance to specific conditions, while §283 allows such damages when the debtor is no longer obligated to perform. This could lead to ambiguity about when damages are applicable.

§280 allows damages for breach of duty, while §281 allows damages instead of performance. Both can apply under different conditions, but their overlap may lead to double recovery or unclear prioritization.
§283 enables damages instead of performance under certain conditions, and §280 governs general damages for breach. Their interplay may lead to ambiguity about when one applies over the other.

§285 allows the creditor to demand the return of an 'Ersatz' or assignment of an 'Ersatzanspruch', while §326 limits the creditor's obligation to provide 'Gegenleistung' based on the value of the 'Ersatz'. This creates potential ambiguity in how these provisions interact when a creditor exercises the right under §285.

§275 establishes the conditions under which the debtor is excused from performance, and §326 determines the consequences of that excusal. The interplay between these two clauses may lead to conflicting interpretations if the excusal conditions in §275 are not clearly defined in relation to the consequences outlined in §326.

Conflict arises between §326 (which determines when counter-performance is lost) and §275 (which defines when performance is excluded). If the conditions in 275 are interpreted inconsistently with 326, it may lead to unclear obligations regarding counter-performance.

Conflict arises between §326 (which addresses counter-performance) and §285 (which governs the return of indemnities). If the conditions for returning an indemnity in 285 are not aligned with 326's rules on counter-performance, it may lead to ambiguity in the scope of obligations.

Conflict arises between §326 (which allows withdrawal) and §346 (which governs the consequences of withdrawal). If the conditions for withdrawal in 326 are not coordinated with the restitution requirements in 346, it may lead to inconsistencies in how withdrawal impacts obligations.
§311a allows for damages without a prior deadline, while §281 requires a deadline before damages can be claimed. This creates a conflict in procedural requirements.

§311a permits non-performance at contract conclusion, while §275 excludes performance when impossible or disproportionate. The overlap may create ambiguity about whether performance is truly excluded or merely delayed.
§281 requires a deadline before damages can be claimed, while §346 mandates restitution or value compensation without such a condition, creating a potential conflict in remedy application.
§280 provides general damages for breach, while §346 specifies specific restitution or value compensation rules, possibly leading to inconsistent enforcement.

§441 allows for price reduction instead of withdrawal, while §346 mandates value compensation upon withdrawal. This creates potential for conflicting obligations if both provisions are triggered by the same event.

§441 references §347, which requires value compensation for improper use of benefits, but §441 allows for price reduction. This may lead to ambiguity in cases where both improper use and price reduction apply.

§441 allows for price reduction based on value loss, while §346 requires return of performance or value compensation upon withdrawal. These may conflict when a buyer reduces price but also seeks return of performance.
§441 adjusts price based on value at time of contract, while §347 considers usage and improvements after withdrawal. This may lead to conflicting assessments of value when withdrawal occurs.
